items.stem: For an AR(1) process the Yule–Walker estimate of Φ is:
items.explanation: For an AR(1), the Yule–Walker equation is ρ₁=Φρ₀=Φ because ρ₀=1. The method-of-moments estimate is therefore Φ̂=r₁.

items.stem: For an AR(2) with r₁ = 0.5 and r₂ = 0.3, Φ̂₂ is:
In question 2, Φ̂₁ is:
items.explanation: The AR(2) Yule–Walker estimate is Φ̂₁=r₁(1−r₂)/(1−r₁²). Here 0.5×0.7/0.75≈0.4667.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with Φ = 0.6 and σ²_ε = 4, Var(yₜ) is:
items.explanation: A stationary AR(1) has variance σ²ε/(1−Φ²). Thus 4/(1−0.6²)=4/0.64=6.25.

items.stem: The PACF of an AR(2) process satisfies:
items.explanation: For an AR(p), the theoretical PACF cuts off after lag p. With p=2, it is zero at lags 3 and higher.

items.stem: Which of the following AR(2) parameter pairs gives a stationary process?
items.explanation: AR(2) stationarity requires −1<Φ₂<1, Φ₁+Φ₂<1 and Φ₂−Φ₁<1. Only (0.4,0.3) satisfies all three conditions.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with Φ = −0.5, ρ₂ equals:
items.explanation: For an AR(1), ρₖ=Φᵏ. At lag 2, (−0.5)²=0.25.

items.stem: The ACF of an MA(1) process is nonzero:
items.explanation: An MA(q) autocorrelation function cuts off after lag q. For MA(1), only lag 1 can have a non-zero autocorrelation beyond lag zero.

items.stem: For an AR(2), the relation ρ₂ = Φ₁ρ₁ + Φ₂ is obtained by:
options: multiplying the model by yₜ and taking expectation
multiplying by yₜ₋₂ and taking expectation
items.explanation: Multiply the AR(2) equation by yₜ₋₂ and take expectations. The innovation is uncorrelated with past values, yielding ρ₂=Φ₁ρ₁+Φ₂.

items.stem: If for an AR(2) the sample values are r₁ = 0.6, r₂ = 0.36, then Φ̂₂ is:
items.explanation: The AR(2) estimate Φ̂₂ has numerator r₂−r₁². Since 0.36−0.6²=0, the estimate is zero.

items.stem: The spectral density function is the Fourier transform of the:
items.explanation: The spectral density and autocovariance function form a Fourier-transform pair. The spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance sequence.

items.stem: The periodogram as an estimator of the spectral density is:
items.explanation: The raw periodogram is asymptotically unbiased under standard conditions, but it is inconsistent because its variance does not tend to zero as sample size increases.

items.stem: To obtain a consistent estimator of the spectral density one:
options: smooths the periodogram with a window
items.explanation: Smoothing the periodogram with a suitable spectral window averages neighbouring frequencies and reduces variance, producing a consistent spectral-density estimator under standard bandwidth conditions.

items.stem: The spectral density of a white noise process is:
items.explanation: White noise has zero autocovariance at all non-zero lags. Its spectral density is therefore constant across frequency.

items.stem: ∫f(ω)dω over the full range equals:
items.explanation: Under the usual convention f(ω)=(1/2π)Σγₖe^(−iωk), integrating f from −π to π gives γ₀, the variance of the process.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with Φ = 0.8, the spectral density is largest at:
items.explanation: For a stationary AR(1), f(ω) is proportional to 1/(1+Φ²−2Φcosω). With positive Φ, the denominator is smallest at ω=0, so the spectrum peaks at low frequency.

items.stem: The PACF is primarily used to:
options: identify the order of an AR process
items.explanation: The PACF measures the correlation at lag k after controlling for intermediate lags. For an AR(p), its cutoff helps identify p.

items.stem: For yₜ=εₜ−0.7εₜ₋₁ with innovation variance 1, the spectral density is proportional to:
items.explanation: For MA(1), f(ω) is proportional to |1+θe^(−iω)|²=1+θ²+2θcosω under the plus-sign MA convention; for yₜ=εₜ−θεₜ₋₁ it is 1+θ²−2θcosω. With θ=0.7 the latter is 1.49−1.4cosω.

items.stem: Bartlett, Tukey–Hanning and Parzen are names of:
items.explanation: Bartlett, Tukey–Hanning and Parzen are examples of spectral windows (also called lag windows) used to smooth spectral estimates.

items.stem: The cumulative periodogram is used to test whether a series is:
items.explanation: The cumulative periodogram compares cumulative spectral power with the linear pattern expected under white noise. It is used as a diagnostic test for whiteness.

items.stem: The process yₜ = yₜ₋₁ + εₜ is:
items.explanation: The process contains a unit root: shocks accumulate and the variance grows with time. It is a random walk and is not covariance-stationary.

items.stem: For the random walk yₜ=μ+yₜ₋₁+εₜ with y₀=0, E(yₜ) and Var(yₜ) are:
items.explanation: Assuming y₀=0 and zero-mean innovations with variance σ², iteration gives E(yₜ)=tμ and Var(yₜ)=tσ².

items.stem: If Φ₁ + Φ₂ = 1 in an AR(2), the process:
items.explanation: The AR polynomial is 1−Φ₁B−Φ₂B². If Φ₁+Φ₂=1, it has a root at B=1, so the process contains a unit root.

items.stem: For yₜ = 1.2yₜ₋₁ − 0.2yₜ₋₂ + εₜ, the differenced series Δyₜ is:
items.explanation: The AR polynomial factors as 1−1.2B+0.2B²=(1−B)(1−0.2B). After first differencing, (1−0.2B)Δyₜ=εₜ, an AR(1) with coefficient 0.2.

items.stem: An ARIMA(2, 1, 0) process becomes stationary after:
items.explanation: In ARIMA(p,d,q), d is the number of differences applied to the original series. An ARIMA(2,1,0) is differenced once to obtain a stationary AR(2) model.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with Φ = −0.5, the autocorrelations are:
items.explanation: For an AR(1), ρₖ=Φᵏ. A negative coefficient makes the sign alternate with the lag.

items.stem: An MA(1) process yₜ = εₜ − θεₜ₋₁ is invertible if:
items.explanation: For yₜ=εₜ−θεₜ₋₁, invertibility requires the root of 1−θB=0 to lie outside the unit circle, equivalent to |θ|<1.

items.stem: The Dickey–Fuller test is used to test for:
items.explanation: The Dickey–Fuller family of tests examines the null hypothesis that an autoregressive process has a unit root.

items.stem: A sample ACF that decays very slowly and almost linearly suggests:
options: a unit root — difference the series
items.explanation: A very slowly decaying sample ACF is a common symptom of a unit root or near-unit-root behaviour. First differencing is then examined to remove the stochastic trend.

items.stem: For a process with Φ₁ = 0.4, Φ₂ = 0.3, θ₁ = 0.6, θ₂ = 0.4, the process is:
items.explanation: The AR(2) part is stationary because its coefficients satisfy the AR(2) stationarity inequalities. The MA(2) polynomial 1+0.6B+0.4B² has complex roots with modulus √(1/0.4)≈1.58, outside the unit circle, so it is invertible too.

items.stem: For a Gaussian process, weak stationarity implies:
items.explanation: For a Gaussian process, all finite-dimensional distributions are determined by the mean vector and covariance matrix. If the mean is constant and covariance depends only on lag, these distributions are invariant to time shifts, giving strict stationarity.

items.stem: For the random walk yₜ=yₜ₋₁+εₜ with y₀=0 and zero-mean innovations of variance σ², E(yₜ) and Var(yₜ) are:
items.explanation: With y₀=0 and no drift, yₜ is the sum of t independent zero-mean innovations. Its mean is 0 and its variance is tσ².

items.stem: Weak stationarity requires the autocovariance to depend on:
items.explanation: Weak stationarity requires a constant mean and an autocovariance function that depends on the lag, not on calendar time t.

items.stem: A random walk becomes stationary after:
items.explanation: First differencing a random walk gives Δyₜ=εₜ. The differenced series is white noise under the stated innovation assumptions.

items.stem: In a random walk, the effect of a single shock on future values is:
items.explanation: A shock enters every subsequent level of a random walk with coefficient one. Its effect does not decay, so it is permanent.

items.stem: The series yₜ = 5 + 0.2t + εₜ is:
items.explanation: The deterministic component 5+0.2t is a linear trend. Subtracting the fitted deterministic trend leaves εₜ, so the series is trend-stationary rather than stationary in levels.

items.stem: Over-differencing a stationary series produces:
options: a unit root in the AR part
items.explanation: Differencing a stationary series unnecessarily can introduce a non-invertible moving-average component with a unit root, making the model harder to estimate.

items.stem: For a random walk, Corr(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) equals:
items.explanation: For a zero-drift random walk starting at zero, Cov(yₜ,yₜ₊ₖ)=tσ², Var(yₜ)=tσ² and Var(yₜ₊ₖ)=(t+k)σ². Hence the correlation is √[t/(t+k)].

items.stem: ARIMA(0, 1, 0) describes:
items.explanation: ARIMA(0,1,0) has no AR or MA terms after one difference. Thus Δyₜ is white noise and yₜ is a random walk.

items.stem: A random walk with drift is yₜ=0.2+yₜ₋₁+εₜ, with fixed y₀=5 and E(εₜ)=0. What is E(y₁₀)?
items.explanation: Iterating gives yₜ=y₀+0.2t+Σᵢ₌₁ᵗεᵢ. Taking expectations at t=10 gives 5+2=7.
